name: llm-book-mini-project
oneLiner: The companion project to the LangChain book: fourteen stages, each with a contract, and not one of them implemented.
summary: Ops Copilot is meant to be an internal operations assistant: it answers questions about orders and incidents by querying real systems, and it can take exactly one irreversible action — sending an email — only from behind a human approval gate. It is built a stage at a time across the seventeen chapters of `llm-book`, and each stage directory carries a `README.md` stating what that stage must demonstrate and what its tests must prove. **It is a skeleton today: the stage structure and tooling are in place, no stage is implemented**, and the repository says so outright at the top of its README. One rule is worth more than all the rest: **every stage's tests pass without a single real model call.** Not 'mostly', not 'except the integration ones'. A stage that needs a live provider to demonstrate anything has been designed wrong — and the book devotes a chapter to saying so. The second deliverable is the final stage's `DECISIONS.md`, which the repository states plainly matters more than its code.
tests: The tooling is in place — pytest, ruff, mypy in strict mode, a CI gate — and there are exactly zero substantive tests, because there is nothing to test. What each stage directory does carry is a contract stating what its tests will have to prove; a test specification written before the tests.
ci: A single `ci.yml` running the toolchain gate. Stage `00-skeleton` exists precisely to prove that gate is real, and it is the only claim in this repository that can be verified today.

metrics.label: Real model calls in the tests
metrics.value: 0 — that is the rule, not the outcome

components.name: The stage contracts
components.description: Fourteen directories, each with a `README.md` stating what the stage adds and what its tests must prove. The contract is written before the implementation — the same pattern as `docs/SPEC.md` in `listing-search-bench`, applied to teaching material.

components.name: The toolchain gate
components.description: uv, ruff, mypy in strict mode and pytest, wired into one workflow. The zeroth stage exists to prove the gate is real before anything starts passing through it.

components.name: The zero-model-call rule
components.description: Stated as a project rule rather than a performance goal: the suite should be fast enough to run on every save, deterministic enough to bisect, and honest enough that a green build means something.

components.name: The decision log as the deliverable
components.description: The final stage is to produce a `DECISIONS.md`: the choice, the rejected alternative, the reason and the cost. The repository says outright that a reviewer reads that document and nobody reads the code.

overlaps.reason: This is that book's companion project and its only executable artefact. The chapters reference the stages, so an unfinished skeleton is a hole in the book rather than a separate repository of no consequence.
The same pairing: a book plus a project meant to prove it. Worth deciding once whether every book in the portfolio carries an executable companion, because today the answer differs from book to book.
Stage 11 is to add a twenty-case evaluation set with a regression threshold in CI. That is exactly the method the other repository has already implemented — no reason to write it a second time here.

product: A channel, and one carrying debt: the book is public and points at a project that is empty. This repository's value will not be its code but its `DECISIONS.md` — the document explaining why a single agent rather than a supervisor, why an idempotency key rather than a distributed transaction, why SSE rather than WebSockets. Documents like that are scarce online, and they are the ones that get cited.
highlights: The 'zero real model calls in the tests' rule, stated without exceptions. Most projects of this kind start with that rule and lose it at the first hard stage; here it is written down as a design condition before anything exists.

Every stage has a contract written before the implementation, saying what it must demonstrate and what its tests must prove. A skeleton with fourteen contracts is worth considerably more than a skeleton with fourteen empty directories.
The status is stated honestly in the README's first paragraph. The repository does not pretend to be further along than it is — and for the companion to a public book that is the only right call.
gaps: **No stage is implemented.** Fourteen contracts and no code, against a book that is already public and already points at them.
The last commit is from 5 August 2026. The repository stands exactly where the skeleton was put down.
The `DECISIONS.md` the repository calls its most important deliverable does not exist — and it is the one thing that could be written now, without implementing anything.
Stage 11 plans an evaluation set with a regression threshold — the method from `agent-eval-bench`, repeated for a third time in this portfolio.
next: Implement stages 00–02. The three simplest stages turn the repository from a skeleton into something a reader of the book can run, and that is the whole difference.
Write `DECISIONS.md` now, from the decisions already made while designing the stages. It needs no implementation at all and it is the stated principal deliverable.
Add a visible note about the companion project's status to the book's README, so a reader does not land in an empty directory without warning.

Rather than writing the evaluation from scratch in stage 11, import the method from `agent-eval-bench` and describe the differences — better teaching material than a third implementation of the same thing.
risks: A public book pointing at an empty repository works against the credibility of both. It is the only entry in this pass where delay costs something already published.
headline: Fourteen stage contracts, zero implementation — against a book that is already public
